written. ‒ the tobacco industry is now one of the largest in the world and brings in huge financial revenues, contributing to the strong growth of the economies of many countries around the world. however, the illicit trade in tobacco products is also widespread. such illegal trade, in particular the smuggling of counterfeit cigarettes, results in losses of revenues for the european union and its member states, amounting to more than eur 10 billion a year when unpaid customs duties, taxes and excise duties are taken into account. the tobacco products directive provides for a legal obligation, which will enter into force by 2019 at the latest, requiring tobacco companies to establish and maintain a system for tracing and tracing tobacco products. however, it is essential that the commission take measures to ensure the full transposition of the tobacco products directive into the national legislation of all member states of the european union and that the commission focus on european and international legislative instruments in order to tackle smuggled and counterfeited cigarettes more effectively. i agree that member states must implement the tobacco products directive in a timely manner and in particular the measures relating to the tracing and tracing of tobacco products. i also think it is wrong that the annual payments of the tobacco industry partly finance the budget of the european anti-fraud office, because such activity can lead to conflicts of interest.
written. ‒ i believe that tobacco fraud affects public health and poses an even greater health risk than original tobacco products because counterfeit cigarettes are produced and imported illegally and use unknown ingredients. i maintain that the central objective of this agreement is to reduce the presence of smuggled tobacco products in the illicit tobacco market in the european union. i stress that the european commission must look for ways to deal with the current situation in a transparent and responsible manner with the involvement of the european parliament. therefore, i consider that all arguments for and against the extension of the agreement with philip morris international should be taken into account as its extension marks a transitional arrangement to prevent a regulatory vacuum until the tobacco products directive fully enters into force.

president-in-office of the council.– mr president, let me start by thanking you for the continuous and constructive contribution of the european parliament to the advancement of montenegro’s accession process to the european union and, in particular, your rapporteur charles tannock. over the past year, relations between the european union and montenegro have maintained a positive momentum. in its conclusions adopted in december last year, the council welcomed the continued progress. it took positive note of improvements in the legal framework in the area of the rule of law and work on the establishment of new institutions. now the council also noted with satisfaction montenegro’s positive role in further developing regional cooperation and in advancing good neighbourly relations. it also commended montenegro for its cooperation on foreign policy issues, in particular, for its continued full alignment with the eu’s foreign policy positions. it is furthermore encouraging evidence that two further negotiation chapters could be opened up at the accession conference in december, bringing the total number of chapters now opened to 22 out of 35. looking to the future, we need to stress again the importance of the rule of law, which is a fundamental value of the european union and a cross cutting concern for the enlargement process. as your draft resolution rightly points out, further progress in montenegro’s accession negotiations continues to depend on progress in this area. the council also restated how important it is for the entire rule of law system to deliver concrete results, in particular, by establishing a solid track record in the fight against corruption and organised crime. further efforts are needed to focus on effective reform implementation, leading to tangible results towards the interim benchmarks. the council will continue to closely monitor developments in this area. on a related note, the council shares the view expressed in your draft resolution that montenegro should intensify its efforts to guarantee freedom of expression and of the media, to pursue the public administration reform and to strengthen the independence of institutions, as well as to improve the business environment. your draft resolution spells out many other important concerns to address, which are also highlighted by the findings of the commission’s progress report. with the upcoming parliamentary elections in montenegro this year, i would stress that ensuring the full implementation of the new electoral legislation is crucial. we are well aware that montenegro currently is facing a difficult political situation and that this could hamper the reform efforts. therefore, it is important to recall the need for all political parties to show responsibility and to re-engage in constructive dialogue, with parliament being the key forum for political debate. in this context, we count on the government and on the opposition to work together, not least to meet the expectations of the montenegrin citizens. this is also important for ensuring public trust in the political process and in the state institutions. sustainable and constructive cooperation remains essential to maintaining the necessary political commitments to effectively address outstanding challenges, to deliver on the reform agenda and to progress in the accession negotiations. dialogue and inclusiveness are also key issues raised by your draft resolution, and i would like to stress how valuable it is that this message is passed on to montenegro. in this respect the european parliament’s important contribution through its work in the stabilisation and association parliamentary committee is most welcome. mr president, let me conclude by saying that, looking ahead, we do hope to see continued progress.

achieving lasting reforms, through the adoption of legislation and the establishment of institutions. as you also point out however – and as the commission stated in its november report – this is not the whole story. our assessment is, unfortunately, that real progress on the ground on the rule of law remains limited, including in establishing a track record in the fight against corruption and the rule of law criteria; they are preconditions for attracting investment, improving competitiveness and stimulating growth and jobs. and therefore, as you know, i prefer to talk about the accession madam president, ladies and gentlemen, this regulation governs the distribution and use of veterinary medicines, but my focus was on combating antimicrobial resistance. it is important that the regulation contains a provision to ban certain antibiotics in veterinary medicine in order to preserve them for human use. but for that to make sense, it has to be retroactive, so it has to include an obligation to withdraw from the market those spare antibiotics that are already on the market. furthermore, it is essential to link the distribution of antibiotics to a prescription issued by an authorised person. also, to prevent possible misuse in the interest of public health, the online sale of antibiotics should be prohibited. human and animal health are increasingly linked through our dietary habits and intensive farming methods, and therefore the antibiotic problem must be addressed through a 'one health' approach. the alarm bells have long been ringing, and future generations may wonder if it's possible that we have ruined one of the greatest achievements in medical science for profit. through this law, the european union has a unique opportunity to contribute to the global effort to preserve the efficacy of antibiotics. in conclusion, i believe that the proposal for a regulation coming from parliament is well designed and will contribute to better protection of animal and human health.
mr. chairman, the role of a whistleblower is of immense importance to any society. it's about the most responsible and courageous individuals who alert the problem before it becomes insoluble. unfortunately, they rarely get the recognition they deserve, and much more often, with their health in jeopardy and disappointed in the system, they leave their jobs within a year or two. in countries where the rule of law is shaken, systemic failings and corruption make it almost impossible for whistleblowers to find genuine satisfaction. whereas in many developed countries, they have a very hard time getting the best lawyers because they prefer to have wealthy corporations as their clients who don't want to work with those who represent whistleblowers. we also often see politicians flirting with whistle-blowers because they have a high moral standing in the public eye and they make easy political points. i think that the policy towards whistle-blowers should be much more constructive and responsible, because they are the ones who point out what needs to be fixed, and because of their experience and knowledge of the internal situation, they often offer concrete, quality solutions. for all this, we need to strongly promote the positive role of whistle-blowers in society, and our states need to do everything possible to ensure that the best legal assistance is available to them at all times. we must also be prepared to offer whistle-blowers from third countries asylum in the european union to protect them and their families from reprisals and possible harm.

written. ‒ banking union is a fundamental element of economic and monetary union, necessary for stability and confidence in banks in the european union. in addition to the single banking union regulation, a single supervisory mechanism (ssm), a single resolution mechanism (srm) and a common deposit insurance scheme (cds) have been established to ensure effective fiscal protection at the level of the european union. the first pillar of the ssm banking union aims to ensure a uniform supervision of eu banks, to contribute to the security and stability of credit institutions and the financial system, and to establish a level playing field in the banking market. the second pillar of the srm guarantees a joint decision-making process for the resolution of failing banks. the third pillar is currently working on harmonising national deposit insurance schemes and may over time guarantee the same level of protection for all deposits in the eu, regardless of location. to avoid new cases of large-scale bank bailouts, to restore investor confidence and to support growth and financial stability, we need to aim for higher and better quality bank capital and a stabilised supervisory and regulatory framework. i welcome the annual report on the banking union, and in particular the establishment of the ssm, which has proved to be a highly successful operation from an operational point of view. in view of the short timeframe for establishment and the complexity of the project, i fully support the report and look forward to the future successes of the banking union.

member of the commission.– madam president, i would like first of all to congratulate ms sylvie goulard for taking the initiative to present this report. last october the commission released a communication aiming at a more unified external representation of our economic and monetary union in international financial institutions. we can no longer accept that the euro area, which has the second largest currency in the world and which represents one of the world’s key market actors and economic powerhouses, does not speak with one voice on economic and financial matters in international financial institutions. this especially holds for the international monetary fund. the international monetary fund is a key pillar of the international monetary system in charge of global crisis prevention and crisis response. it is of strong relevance for the euro area. a more unified representation will allow the euro area to effectively shape its future role in the global financial architecture and more effectively promote euro area interests at a global level. our proposal consists of two elements: streamlining euro area representation in the short term and moving to a unified representation by the year 2025. we are aware that the road ahead is not easy. we are currently discussing the proposals with the member states. the decision-making process will take some time: agreement is not imminent, but we believe that an agreement can be reached. we welcome an early discussion with parliament on this important subject and we take note of your recommendations. we appreciate that the report stresses the need for a stronger european voice. as regards international standard-setting bodies for financial regulation, the situation is very diverse from the financial stability board to the basel committee and others. each body has its own particular governance arrangements, and the extent to which the eu is represented varies – often with only certain member states represented. we agree with parliament that the european position should be better coordinated, as we all understand that when we are united we are stronger on the international scene, and we set out in our october communication what the commission will do to get there. the commission also takes note of the proposals in the report to involve european supervisory authorities more in international fora. a core interest of the european parliament is to be more involved in discussions leading up to the development of new international rules concerning the financial sector. since the entry into force of the lisbon treaty, the commission has been steadily building up strong relations with the committee on economic and monetary affairs (econ). this work is not finished, and we stand ready to provide timely updates on salient developments in international financial regulation. to conclude, a point on the g20: we should bear in mind that the g20 is an informal forum where leaders written. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the proposal for a council directive amending directive 2006/112/ec on the common system of value added tax, as regards the duration of the obligation to respect the minimum standard rate, given that the minimum standard rate currently applied in all member states constitutes a useful safeguard for the proper functioning of the internal market. the existing system of a minimum standard rate of 15% gives member states room to manoeuvre in implementing vat reforms. the decision to set the standard rate at no less than 15% from 1 january 2016 to 31 december 2018 ensures the necessary period for the definitive vat system for intra-eu trade that the commission intends to propose and the reforms that the commission intends to bring to bear to adapt the existing vat rate regulations, i.e. the establishment of a definitive system based on the principle of destination rather than origin.
written. ‒ the vat directive provides that from 1 january 2011 to 31 december 2015 the standard rate shall not be less than 15%. the report proposes extending the time frame to two years, i.e. until 31 december 2017. the minimum rate of vat applies because vat is still charged at the place of origin of the products, rather than at the place of destination, and serves as a safety net for the proper functioning of the internal market. the report proposes to extend the timeframe for the duration of the standard rate of 15%, which will ensure further development and stability in the internal market, and i therefore supported the report.
written. ‒ the minimum standard vat rate of 15% has been in place for years and, with this proposal to amend the vat directive, the european parliament proposes to use it until 31 december 2018. the vat directive provides that the standard rate cannot be less than 15%. the commission notes that the tax exemption for the purposes of article 107 (1) tfeu is not a tax measure that is directly linked to the taxable person's activity. it is also not an ambitious scheme to replicate the existing system, and given that in all member states the standard rate is currently higher than 15%, it also gives member states room for manoeuvre by allowing them to implement vat reforms aimed at reducing the standard rate by broadening the vat base and limiting the application of reduced rates. in view of the above possibilities, i stress the need to apply flexibility mechanisms at national level, especially in the food production sector, with the aim of raising the purchasing power of citizens, but also to help the crisis-hit agricultural sector. for all the above reasons, i supported the amendment to the directive in question.
written. ‒ with a view to establishing the internal market, the commission presented on 1 january 1993 proposals for the establishment of a definitive system of tax harmonisation. given that all member states currently have a standard rate in force of more than 15%, the existing system of a minimum standard rate of 15% also gives member states room for manoeuvre by allowing them to implement vat reforms aimed at reducing the standard rate by broadening the vat base and limiting the application of reduced rates. on 6 december 2011, the commission adopted a communication on the future of vat, which proposed that the country of origin principle cease to apply and described several ways in which taxation could be achieved at the place of destination. the commission will publish in 2016 an action plan for a simple and effective final vat system that is fraud-proof and fit for the single market. i agree with the commission's proposal to retain the principle of a minimum standard vat rate of 15% retroactively and to propose to extend the application of the existing rules for three years (until 31 december 2018).

written. ‒ in january 1993, the commission proposed the harmonisation of the tax system throughout the european union with a view to creating a single market. however, this commission proposal could not be adopted by the council at that time and it decided to adopt a transitional form on the collection of value added tax. this has allowed the movement of goods within the single market, whereby such movement of goods is no longer considered to be an import or an export. in order to ensure the efficient functioning of the single market, directive 92/77/eec sets a minimum rate of vat. on that basis, the standard rate shall not be less than 15%. the provisions of that directive were to apply until december 2015. on 14 december 2015, the commission proposed to amend directive 2006/112/ec in order to extend the application of those rates until december 2017. i support this commission proposal because i believe that in practice the minimum standard rate of 15% has proved to be a good instrument for the functioning of the single market, which is also one of the eu's most important objectives.
written. ‒ the minimum standard rate applicable in all member states, i.e. the vat directive, which provides that from 1 january 2016 until december 2018 the standard rate of vat shall not be lower than 15%, is a useful safeguard mechanism for the proper functioning of the internal market. this sixth extension of the standard vat rate maintains the current situation, provides legal certainty for shareholders and allows the entry into force of a definitive vat system for intra-union trade. i am extremely positive about the harmonisation of legislation on turnover taxes to the extent necessary to ensure the establishment and functioning of the internal market and to avoid distortions of competition. given that the commission intends to publish in 2016 an action plan for a simple and efficient final vat system that will be fraud-proof and fit for the single market, it seems appropriate to maintain the principle of the minimum standard rate currently in force.

the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) is a form of assistance to people who have lost their jobs as a result of the effects of globalisation, structural change or the economic crisis. the purpose of the egf is to enable the unemployed to find work as quickly as possible, but it can also serve the self-employed, temporary and fixed-term workers. the egf may be used to provide assistance for counselling, vocational training and education, and the creation of entrepreneurial and business opportunities. in september 2015, sweden submitted an application for a financial contribution from the egf in order to make redundancies in 647 workers, 470 of whom were declared technically surplus at the company volvo trucks. the main reason for the redundancies is the emergence of asian truck manufacturers, which forces volvo trucks to reduce costs and increase efficiency in order to compete. the egf will be used to support the development of the social economy and the social inclusion of disadvantaged groups, including those who are disadvantaged in their economic and social development. i supported the report because i believe that the egf is a key instrument to help redundant workers and to respond to global challenges.

written. ‒ glyphosate is a non-selective herbicide that acts by affecting the so-called 'slant pathway', which is also present in algae, bacteria and fungi. populations are primarily exposed if they live near the sprayed areas, through household use and through food. the effects of glyphosate on human health should not be underestimated. a number of member states have already taken precautionary measures to protect public health and the environment. since, in the event of an authorisation of an active substance, clear and legally binding conditions for its use should be set at union level in order to achieve an equivalent level of protection in all member states, i invite the commission to mandate its food and veterinary office to test and monitor glyphosate residues in food and drink produced in the union as well as in imported products.

written. ‒ the most widely produced herbicide in the world today is the systemic herbicide glyphosate, whose use has increased dramatically over the last 40 years. glyphosate is a non-selective herbicide, meaning it destroys all plants, and its residues have been found in water, soil, food and drink, as well as in the human body. the impact of glyphosate on the environment and on human and animal health is also unquestionable. the european parliament considers that the draft commission implementing regulation does not apply the precautionary principle and does not provide a high level of protection of human and animal health and the environment. in view of the deficiencies mentioned, the european parliament requests the commission to withdraw its draft implementing regulation and to submit a new one to the committee.
written. glyphosate, which was introduced in 1974, is the most widely used herbicide in the world, and it can enter our bodies through the food we eat, which is unknown to many people. the british food safety authority estimated that a third of all bread was contaminated with traces of glyphosate. similarly, the americans claim that 90 percent of the soybeans they produce are contaminated with glyphosate, and the germans say that every other beer is contaminated with the herbicide. a german study in 18 european countries found the presence of a toxic glyphosate-based herbicide in the urine of 44% of europeans. the presence of trace amounts of glyphosate in our bodies is a concern because this herbicide has been linked to a number of health problems, from metabolic problems to liver and kidney disease to cancer. the world health organization considers glyphosate to be 'probably carcinogenic to humans', while the european food safety authority considers glyphosate to be unlikely to be carcinogenic to humans. i voted in favor of the amendment extending the use of glyphosate to a maximum of seven years, and i supported that objection.
written. ‒ experts have been warning for years about the harmful effects of glyphosate, the world's most widely used herbicide, whose use has increased dramatically over the past 40 years. glyphosate is the most widely used agricultural chemical used in almost all herbicides. given that glyphosate and its residues are found in water, soil, food and drink, inedible products and the human body, i believe that more attention should be paid to its effects on human health. the world health organization claims that glyphosate probably has carcinogenic potential and has been classified as a human carcinogen, while the european food safety authority claims that glyphosate does not pose a risk to humans because of its carcinogenic potential. although the two organizations mentioned have opposing views, i believe that there should be a high level of protection, both for human and animal health and the environment, and i voted to not renew the approval of glyphosate.

member of the commission.– madam president, this discussion illustrated very well all the difficult questions and dilemmas that we had while working on this new legislation for the protection of the private data of eu citizens. i would like to mention some of the big dilemmas that we had when we were seeking a proper and right balance for our solutions. one of those dilemmas is a big question these days – the dilemma between privacy and security – and many of you mentioned it here today. this is a question that everybody has to reply to personally because it is a very private question: to what extent am i willing to give up my privacy in the interests of being more secure? this is the basic question, and very probably i will answer myself as a person who lived part of my life under a totalitarian regime, when i knew i was being spied on by state police. my reply will probably be different – because i am more sensitive about this – to the reply of the young people sitting over there in the audience who have not had such an experience. now we are preparing the legislation which will balance this properly for everybody in europe. this is a really difficult task, and especially these days we must be aware that after every new terrorist attack people will be more and more willing to give up their privacy in the interests of security. that is why we must be so vigilant and careful and protect fundamental rights and the right to privacy. so we are in a situation where we have to let law enforcement bodies act properly, using data in the necessary and proportionate way – and this is the formulation that the supreme courts use when identifying the balance and the right of access to data on the part of law enforcement authorities. so we are now in a very sensitive period when we must be especially careful about the protection of privacy and private data. the other dilemma which was also mentioned here, i think by mr polčák, concerns the issue of paternalism – whether the individual has to be responsible, or whether he or she should rely on the public sphere to care for his or her protection. i mentioned that the commission will work very strongly and intensively on guiding people on how to use their new rights. we will always stress that individual people should be the first to care about their privacy and their private data, and we will warn them not to send data to places, especially in digital sphere, where their privacy might be endangered. then the secondary measure is legislation. there is no legislation which can protect the privacy of people 100%, and we must be clear about that and also educate people in europe to be and to retain the position of ‘data subjects’ and not to become ‘data objects’ who expect others to protect them. i think this is very important. the third dilemma is between opening and keeping a space for innovation, and protection. you know that the digital sphere in particular is the sphere where technology is driven by the economy, by big business interests, and here we see that the law comes third and is the slowest. so this is what we need to do now, to catch up with this sphere of economy and technology while keeping a free space for innovation which is so necessary for economic growth and filtering out the risks in that sphere for individual people, and to act only there in that sphere of possible risk and to offer the proper instruments to protect people’s privacy. i also admire the fact – and i think it was mr de kerchove who mentioned it here – that the directive from 1995 proved to be future-proof. look at it: it was created before the digital boom, and still we use this directive. but we all know that we need to come up with a new set of rules which will be unified for the whole of europe, because digital does not like borders and we have the duty to remove borders. here i come to what you mentioned in relation to the rest of the world. i am convinced that this unified and unique set of rules for the eu will lead to the eu becoming the world leader, setting the standards also for the rest of the world. we will have to review all our adequacy decisions which relate to the transfer of european citizens’ data to third countries. this is the hot topic of today, which some of you mentioned as well, and i would like to use this opportunity to inform you about the position of the commission on today’s opinion of working party 29, because this working party, which brings together the data protection authorities from all the member states, today published its opinion on the results of our negotiations on the new regime for data transfers to the united states. it was mentioned several times, so i will use this opportunity to give you, for the first time, the commission’s reaction. i would like to say that, as we understand it, the european data protection authorities, i.e. the article 29 working party, today welcomed the significant improvements that the commission has obtained in two years of negotiations, leading to the eu/us privacy shield, compared to the old safe harbour framework, especially regarding the transparency of the arrangement and safeguards for national security access. the data protection authorities also mentioned some areas that should be further clarified in the commission’s draft adequacy decision. so the commission will now examine the opinion in depth and address the working party’s recommendations in its final decision. i already discussed this with ms falque-pierrotin, chair of the article 29 working party, when i spoke with her by phone earlier today before this plenary session. one point i can mention is that the commission will produce a citizen’s guide to make sure that individuals have easy-to-understand, practical information on how to obtain redress in case of complaints. the next step is for the member states to discuss and vote on the privacy shield in a committee of experts, the so-called article 31 committee. the first discussion will take place on 29 april. as i said before, my aim is that we can put the new arrangement in place by june. we urgently need strong protections for our citizens whose data is transferred across the atlantic, and we need legal certainty for the many european companies that carry out transfers to the united states as part of their business operations.

written. the issue of the collection, processing and use of personal data has taken on a new dimension with the development of information technology. today, in our business and personal lives, we are constantly exposed to digital technology. the digital environment is constantly circulating, collecting, storing and recording information that is also personal. the fact is that the process of change in the social and economic environment through the use of digital technology is much faster than the legislative adaptations that regulate the new possible forms of abuse. the outdated directive 95/46/ec (general data protection regulation) is no longer able to adequately regulate and protect human rights in the light of all the changes that have taken place with the development of information technology. the new regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data and repealing directive 95/46/ec (general data protection regulation) provides an excellent basis for the protection of personal data and personal identity in the digital environment. the new regulation creates an enabling environment for the development of the economy and the digital society in the future.

written. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament's draft legislative resolution on the council's position at first reading with a view to adopting a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data and repealing directive 95/46/ec (general data protection regulation), given that we are finally getting one of the elements amending directive 95/46. such an outdated directive was no longer able to regulate and protect human rights in an appropriate way in the light of all the changes that have taken place with the development of information technology. today we live in a digital society that seeks new solutions that will reconcile both the needs of citizens for privacy protection and the opportunities for further development of an economy that is increasingly based on digital technology. this provides an advanced standard, an advanced solution that can become a model for legislation beyond the eu. this solution represents a balance between consumer rights and the needs of business operators. it is the foundation for the protection of human rights, because the protection of personal data is the protection of personal identity. the commission notes that the measure is not intended to create a new legal framework for the digital economy.
written. ‒ i welcome the introduction of new legal frameworks in the area of personal data protection, as this will raise the level of security within the european union's borders and prevent any misuse of our citizens' personal data in advance. i agree that the european union's policy based on the right to protection of personal data needs to be strengthened, because it is this principle that guides the european union, that everyone has the right to the protection of his or her identity. i believe that the implementation of this proposal will lead to significant improvements in terms of legal certainty, reduction of administrative burden and consistency of data protection implementation in the union, all the more so as it protects the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons, and in particular the right to the protection of personal data. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council should be given the opportunity to discuss the issue of the protection of personal data in the context of the european union's new millennium. the measures also call on member states to establish better communication with each other to make the system fully functional, and i believe that better communication and cooperation will result.
written. ‒ the adoption of this regulation, which i support, completes the complete reform of the data protection rules that the ep has been working on for four years. the reform will replace the current data protection directive dating back to 1995 when the internet was in its infancy, and a general regulation designed to give citizens greater control over their own information in the digitised world of smartphones, social media and online banking. the new rules include, among other things, the right to erasure (the 'right to be forgotten'), 'clear and affirmative consent' to the processing of personal data by the data subject, the right to transfer data to another controller, the notification of data subjects about a personal data breach, ensuring that privacy rules are explained in clear and understandable language and stronger enforcement of fines for companies up to 4% of their total annual worldwide turnover if they breach the rules. this is a great success for the european parliament and a loud european 'yes' to strong consumer rights and competition in the digital age. citizens will be able to decide for themselves what personal information they want to share.

written. ‒ under the provisions of this directive, member states will have to set up a 'passenger information unit' (piu) to manage the pnr data collected from air carriers. the data would be retained for a period of five years: in the original form for the first six months, and then 'hidden', meaning that certain data from which the data subject could be directly identified, such as name, address and contact details, would be hidden. the directive states that such transfers should be carried out only on a 'case-by-case' basis and exclusively for the specific needs of 'the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of terrorist offences or serious criminal offences'. the directive will apply to all flights from third countries to the eu and vice versa, as well as to flights within the eu. if a member state decides to apply this directive to intra-eu flights, it shall inform the commission in writing. the eu member states may choose to collect and process pnr data from travel agencies and tour operators providing travel-related services, including flight reservations, for which they collect and process pnr data. i consider the reason for adopting this legislative package to be proportionate to the risks we face and i expect full respect for human rights in its implementation.

written. ‒ pnr data help law enforcement authorities in the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of serious crime, including terrorist offences, as it can be compared with various databases of wanted persons and cases in order to gather evidence and, if necessary, find accomplices and uncover criminal networks. the commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 26 to supplement this regulation by laying down detailed rules for the application of this regulation. member states shall ensure that, in accordance with their national law, dissuasive, effective and proportionate penalties, including fines, are imposed on air carriers and non-air carriers which fail to transmit data required by this directive to the extent that they have already collected them or do not transmit them in an appropriate format, if they do not process them in accordance with the data protection rules laid down in this directive. member states may also continue to apply bilateral or multilateral agreements or mutual arrangements on the exchange of information between competent authorities where those agreements or arrangements are compatible with this directive. the pnr data can be a useful tool for the effective prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of terrorist offences and serious crime, thereby enhancing internal security.

written. ‒ i voted in favour of the draft legislative resolution of the european parliament on the proposal for a directive of the parliament and of the council on the protection of undisclosed know-how and business information (trade secrets) against their unauthorised disclosure, use or disclosure, as i believe that an appropriate balance needs to be struck between the protection of trade secrets and fundamental rights. trade secrets are of particular importance for smes and so-called start-ups, given that they often lack the specialised human resources and financial resources to protect their intellectual property rights in an appropriate manner. globalisation has made trade secrets increasingly vulnerable to fraud, theft and espionage, and there is a growing possibility that those secrets may be misused in third countries. i consider that the differences in the member states' legislation on this matter lead to an uneven level of protection of trade secrets and consequently to the fragmentation of the internal market. i believe that the harmonisation of european trade secret law will improve conditions in the sector concerned and therefore i support this report.
written. ‒ businesses and research institutions are constantly investing financial resources and time in acquiring, developing and applying knowledge and information. information and knowledge are key to the development of a knowledge-based and innovation-driven economy and thus provide an advantage over other competitors. information and achievements can be protected by patents, copyrights, and design rights. in addition to 'visible' information and achievements, companies may also possess so-called trade secrets which are strictly confidential and their availability is very limited. the commission has not found that the information provided by the applicant is sufficient to establish that the product concerned is not covered by the scope of the investigation. the protection of trade secrets against their unlawful acquisition, use or disclosure is key to operating in a dynamic business environment for all companies and research institutions. i supported this report because it defines the appropriate level of protection and the importance of trade secrets in a business environment.
written. ‒ i supported the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the protection of undisclosed know-how and business information (trade secrets) against their unauthorised acquisition, use or disclosure. the question of the protection of trade secrets is crucial for the success of a given undertaking on the market and its competitiveness in the market competition, but at the same time it is also a challenge for the policy of both recruiting and retaining quality workers within a given undertaking. i support the proposal for a common definition of a trade secret and for laying down general principles applicable to member states in terms of enforcement instruments which should prevent the disclosure of trade secrets. the protection procedures should not be administratively burdensome and care should also be taken to protect business secrets during possible litigation. finally, i would point out that employees should not be prevented from using their experience and skills when changing jobs. it is labour mobility that is key to the eu's competitive economy, and the exchange of knowledge and work experience throughout a career contributes to the success of the individual and the companies in which he or she works.
written. ‒ the proposal on the protection of trade secrets against unauthorised acquisition, use or disclosure is particularly important for identifying rules that improve the competitiveness of european companies through innovation and, more broadly, enhance the image of the european union as a world market leader in the industrial sector. in the process of exploring and creating new ideas, products and services, there is a lot of information that is necessary to maximise future competitiveness, therefore trade secrets, their acquisition, use and disclosure need to be protected and regulated at european level. the commission should be able to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 tfeu in order to amend this directive by amending the annex to directive (eu) 2016/797. in view of the above, i welcome this directive of the european parliament.
written. ‒ the proposal for a directive introduces a very broad definition of trade secrets and there is a risk that certain criminal business activities will be protected by this directive. the public interest was jeopardized because the whistleblower was not adequately protected. this directive confers an exclusive right to secrecy on businesses, thus undermining the fundamental freedoms against the protection of business secrets. the directive also interferes in several areas, such as the right of access to information, insufficient protection for whistleblowers, the possibility for workers to change jobs because of the possible disclosure of a trade secret. the proposal for a directive can be linked to the recent negotiations on trade secrets under the ttip. there's a trade secret initiative in the united states at the federal level. the proposal for a directive has been criticised by civil society and journalists, and an online petition has been launched, with over 150 000 signatures so far, to protect whistleblowers at european level. recent scandals, like luxleaks and the panama papers, have highlighted the importance of whistleblowers and investigative journalism to the public interest. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of whistleblowers, the protection of the public interest by denying access to information and the sending of the wrong political message following the recent panama papers scandal.
written. ‒ europe is committed to promoting science and innovation and has the potential to become a world leader in this area. the level of r&d undertaken by companies within the union is, however, insufficient compared to some of the main trading partners, in particular the usa and japan. improving the conditions for innovative business activities is necessary, and the commission has therefore committed itself, within the framework of the wider europe 2020 strategy, to creating an innovation union by protecting investment in fundamental knowledge and creating an innovation-friendly environment in europe. intellectual property rights are a key part of innovation policy and seek to protect creative or creative endeavours. trade secrets are of particular importance for the protection of non-technological innovations. however, the current unevenness and fragmentation of the legal framework on the protection of trade secrets prevents the internal market from functioning effectively. it is essential to improve the intellectual property infrastructure and to review the protection of trade secrets while making relevant information available to the citizens of the european union. in view of the above, i support this report.
written. ‒ i voted in favour of the proposal on the protection of undisclosed know-how and business information (trade secrets) against their unauthorised acquisition, use or disclosure. the commission should be able to impose a maximum period of five years for the submission of such requests, provided that the conditions laid down in this regulation are met. the commission should be able to assess the impact of trade secrets on the protection of intellectual property rights and the protection of intellectual property rights in the union. i consider it appropriate to define at union level the situations in which the acquisition, use and disclosure of a trade secret is authorised or unauthorised and that it is necessary to limit the period of legal protection in order to allow this directive to fulfil its objective of the consistent protection of trade secrets in the european union.

written. ‒ the manipulation of libor and euribor interest rates and foreign exchange benchmarks, as well as alleged manipulation of other indices, have highlighted the importance of benchmarks and their sensitivity. the commission should also be able to assess the impact of the benchmarking exercise on the benchmark benchmark benchmark. the commission should be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 tfeu concerning the establishment of a european data protection supervisor. in response to those publications, the european union has supplemented the existing proposal for a market abuse regulation (mar) by clarifying that the manipulation of benchmarks is illegal and subject to criminal sanctions. however, this does not remove the risk of manipulation resulting from inappropriate management of the benchmarking process. i therefore welcome the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council which aims to improve the governance and control of the benchmarking process. i would stress that it is of the utmost importance to ensure and improve the functioning of the internal market and thus to guarantee a high level of consumer and investor protection and to increase transparency for the sake of financial market stability.
written. ‒ reference interbank interest rates, such as libor (the daily rate at which banks offer money to each other for borrowing on the london interbank market) and euribor (the reference interest rate set on the european interbank market for the euro) are crucial for market monitoring. the link between those rates and a number of financial transactions affects the profits and losses of investors in financial products and their manipulation can cause significant harm to market confidence, consumers, investors and the real economy. it is therefore necessary to lay down clear rules for the introduction of transparency into the rates used in the european union. furthermore, it is necessary that benchmarks in one member state can be applied in other member states because the harmonised framework reduces differences in the legislation of member states that may create obstacles to the smooth functioning of the internal market for the provision of benchmarks. in the light of the above, i support this report as i believe that a stricter regime is needed for systemically important benchmark rates such as euribor and libor.
written. ‒ in order to ensure the proper functioning of the internal market and to improve the conditions for its functioning, in particular as regards financial markets, and to guarantee a high level of consumer and investor protection, it is necessary to establish a regulatory framework for benchmarks. the financial industry relies on benchmarks to assess the performance of an investment fund in order to monitor returns, determine the allocation of portfolio assets or calculate performance fees. i supported this report because implementation fully respects the independence of the european central bank, but also the independence of the national central banks, which is enshrined in the constitutional structures of the member state or third country concerned.

written. ‒ i supported the resolution on the report on discharge in respect of the implementation of the budget of the european union agencies for the financial year 2014: performance, financial management and control of the eu agencies. the court of auditors' finding indicates that the budget for all agencies in 2014 amounted to around eur 1,9 billion, representing a decrease of around 5% compared to 2013 and around 1,4% of the general budget of the union. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the union's macro-financial assistance to the countries of central and eastern europe, in particular through the european neighbourhood instrument (enpi) and the european neighbourhood instrument (enpi). the agencies do important work and have a direct impact on the daily lives of europe's citizens. i welcome the fact that the final accounts of all decentralised agencies present realistically and objectively, by all relevant parameters, their financial position and the results of their operations and their cash flows in 2014. i also welcome the fact that more than 80% of all decentralised agencies have their own anti-fraud strategies while of the four remaining agencies, three more are due to adopt this strategy document during the year. the principles of 'value for money' and 'eu added value' applicable to all european institutions and agencies should be an additional motivation for transparently informing citizens about their work and the results of the activities they carry out.
written. ‒ i support the report on the performance, financial management and control of eu agencies. the tasks entrusted to the european union agencies are of great importance and have a direct impact on the daily lives of citizens. for this reason, the number of agencies has increased considerably during the last century. i welcome the fact that the final financial statements were drawn up in accordance with the provisions of the applicable financial regulations and the accounting rules adopted by the commission's accounting officer. financial transparency is important to ensure the best possible management of the budget paid by taxpayers. i take note of the benefits that synergies and joint procurement procedures under the common approach bring not only to the agencies but also to the commission. in this context, i regret that the commission is planning to start charging the agencies administrative fees for their services. i would remind the commission that the agencies receive funding from the same union budget and that these fees could result in a weaker participation in joint procurement procedures. i call on the commission to reconsider the introduction of fees for public procurement agencies run by the commission. the commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 concerning the conditions for the participation of the european parliament in the work of the agency. finally, i recognise the role that agencies play in supporting eu policies.

‒ council regulation (ec) no 1225/2009 of 30 november 2009 on protection against dumped imports from countries not members of the european community has been amended several times in the past. a commission decision adopted in 1987 established the rule that after a dozen amendments to a given act, it must be codified, that is to say, the original text in the new edition must be textually cleared of any obsolete wording which has been amended in the meantime, in order to avoid possible confusion and inadvertent application of obsolete rules. given that this is an act containing anti-dumping rules, explaining the procedure for initiating and conducting a dumping investigation, regulating the imposition of provisional measures, the imposition and collection of anti-dumping duties, i consider the proposed codification necessary as it not only contributes to greater legal certainty for the stakeholders concerned but also contributes to the correct application of this act.

written. ‒ the sustainable fisheries partnership agreement with liberia and the eu provides financial and technical support to the eu in exchange for fishing rights for a wide range of fish stocks in liberia's exclusive economic zone. european union fleets have been fishing for tropical tuna in the gulf of guinea since the 1950s and currently account for 10% of the world's tuna catch. the agreement could further extend the network of tuna fisheries agreements in west africa. the new protocol enhances cooperation between the eu and the republic of liberia to promote the development of a sustainable fisheries policy. the fisheries sector currently accounts for 3% of total gdp and has the potential to make a significant contribution to liberia's development. the sectoral support to be made available under the protocol will assist the republic of liberia in implementing its national strategy in the field of fisheries, scientific research, small-scale coastal fishing as well as monitoring, control and surveillance of fisheries and combating illegal fishing, which is why i have supported this report.
written. ‒ this sustainable fisheries partnership agreement is the first that the european union will conclude with the republic of liberia, which has 570 kilometres of coastline along the atlantic ocean. its exclusive economic zone of 246 152 km2 is a habitat for bottom and pelagic fish species, including tuna and tuna-like species. given that the eu and liberia have been cooperating for many years through multilateral agreements and that the liberian authorities are cooperating intensively with the eu in the fight against iuu fishing, i believe that the eu-liberia sustainable fisheries partnership agreement will be beneficial for both parties. the eu vessels may catch 6 500 tonnes of tuna per year for which liberia will receive eur 3,25 million over five years, and liberia shall not provide any other state fishing on the high seas with more favourable conditions than the eu. the financial contribution shall be divided equally between the amount for access to fishery resources and the amount for support to liberia's sectoral fisheries policy. i believe that the positive impact of sectoral support measures on the local economy and the coastal community will be felt in the long term. the accompanying financial packages also contribute to the fight against illegal fishing, which is unfortunately present and which we must combat.

mr president, i would like to remind you, at the outset, that mr juncker recently said in this house that every european has been a refugee at some point in the last 100 years. this is why i am motivated to support any amendment, any improvement and this improvement of the new common asylum policy. the fact is, the depth rule didn't work, so we need to improve it. so i'm all for improving this rule, but we also see the weaknesses that have been there. the smugglers knew that, and we know that, and that is why we have been calling for solidarity and responsibility from day one. today, the word solidarity is being used again, and i hope that it will be the main backbone of this common asylum policy. as far as fines are concerned, i am not in favour of introducing fines and i do not agree with this solution, although i see that unfortunately it may be the only solution. but i'm not personally in favor of that solution. i want to remind you of the large number of unaccompanied minors, and this is 10,000 minors, that is not just a statistic, but a fact, and it's up to us to think about that data. i therefore think that any innovation is welcome and i am in favour of bringing about these changes to the dublin rules and the overall common asylum policy.
mr vice-president, commissioner avramopoulos, i thank mr timmermans for presenting the proposal from the european commission on the reform of the common european asylum system. it is clear that the refugee crisis and the migratory movements of the past year have brought to light all the shortcomings and difficulties that we have in the existing system regulated, above all, by the dublin regulation, which has now proven insufficient for the specific form and intensity of the wave of migration that we have experienced. so it seems to me that, in parallel with what we are doing in the area of foreign and security policy, and in the context of the european agenda on migration, this proposal for reform in several segments of the existing legal system is moving towards the good objective of sharing responsibility, fairly demonstrating the real solidarity of all member states, with corrective mechanisms to ensure a long-term acceptable solution and a genuine european policy. i also call for the strengthening of the european asylum support office, the eu asylum agency and the eurodac system.
mr president, the common european asylum system has shown in recent years all its shortcomings and its complete inadequacy in the face of new circumstances, and it is clear that it needs to be upgraded. but the model proposed by the commission again camouflages the problem rather than tackling it. the problem with the european union is that it has a too liberal asylum policy and avoids addressing the problem of illegal migration. we need to reduce the number of people trying to come to europe illegally, not just deal with redistribution. asylum seekers are free people and should choose their own destiny, just as eu member states are free to choose whom they want to receive. the new commission measures are leading us to the point of absurdity, where we are sending asylum seekers to countries they do not want to go to, but are forced to accept them against the will of their own citizens. it is a severe restriction of freedom and a step in the wrong direction.

written. ‒ the problem of cross-border tax avoidance, aggressive tax planning and harmful tax competition has increased in recent years and has become a focus of attention within the union and at global level. member states should increase the level of human, technical and financial resources dedicated to the automatic exchange of information between tax administrations, as it represents an important instrument in the fight against tax fraud, tax evasion and aggressive tax planning. the commission should be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 tfeu concerning the definition of the concept of 'undertaking' and the definition of the concept of 'undertaking'. the provision of an appropriate level of information to the tax authorities of the member states and the commission and the exchange of that information between them could provide an incentive for groups of mfis to abandon certain practices and pay tax in the country where the value is created. the amendment of this directive will make it mandatory for mne's located in or operating in the eu, with total consolidated revenue equal to or greater than eur 750 000 000, to report by country, which is still subject to automatic data exchange. increasing the transparency of mne groups without undermining the union's competitiveness is an important part of countering tax base reduction and profit shifting and ultimately tax avoidance, which is why i supported this report.

‒ the european market of 500 million consumers with a high purchasing power, which they want to access as quickly and easily as possible, must be organised in such a way as to provide consumers with all the relevant information necessary to make an informed choice. this is precisely the way in which the designation of origin of certain products contributes to the recognition of europe in its diversity and to the promotion of the quality of the products. the 'made in' label, first introduced in 1887, has contributed over the past century to a strong concern by national governments and economic operators for the quality of the products they produce and market, and to consumer perceptions of the country of origin. the label has thus contributed significantly to the branding of the product and to the recognition of certain brands and their products through an acceptable price, the longevity of the product and the guaranteed quality behind the country of origin. aren't these the very ideas that we want to implement today through the circular economy versus the unsustainable consumption system that we're witnessing today? i believe that the responsibility of all the players in the single european market, including consumers, is that the introduction of mandatory country of origin labelling for certain non-agricultural products can help the european economy in the time ahead as an added value for products.

written. ‒ i voted in favour of the draft legislative resolution of the european parliament on the draft council decision on the conclusion, on behalf of the european union, of the protocol on the elimination of illicit trade in tobacco products to the world health organisation framework convention on tobacco control, with the exception of its provisions falling within the scope of title iii of part v of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, as this gives the consent to the conclusion of the agreement. i consider that that protocol contains measures and policies in the area of combating illicit trade in tobacco products which can provide substantial support in addressing this problem. the illegal trade in those products contributes to the loss of revenue for the eu due to non-payment of taxes and customs duties and has an impact on the deterioration of the public health situation. therefore, i support this recommendation.
written. ‒ the first health treaty is called the world health organization framework convention on tobacco control (fctc). the agreement is designed as a key response to the global epidemic of tobacco dependence. the union's contribution to the fight against tobacco smuggling is estimated at eur 5 billion. the protocol on the elimination of illicit trade in tobacco products was drawn up on the basis of the agreement and adopted on 12 november 2012. the protocol constitutes the only multilateral regulatory initiative active in relation to tobacco products. the union signed the 2013 protocol, but 40 countries need to ratify it in order for it to become active and to enter into force. the illicit trade in tobacco products is considered a criminal activity that endangers public health. this increases the availability of cheap and highly hazardous tobacco products. the illicit trade in tobacco products, in addition to its negative health effects, also has a negative financial impact. it causes huge revenue losses due to unpaid customs duties and unpaid taxes. the financial loss is estimated at more than eur 10 billion per year. i supported the draft legislative resolution of the european parliament because i believe that it is necessary to eradicate the illicit trade in tobacco products as it endangers public health and damages the union budget.
written. ‒ illegal trade in tobacco products is damaging the budget of the republic of croatia due to unpaid taxes and duties. for this reason, cooperation between eu member states is essential to tackle this problem as effectively as possible, and i therefore consider it very important that the european union urgently ratifies the world health organisation's protocol to combat illicit trade in tobacco. suppressing or reducing illegal sales and increasing prices would reduce consumption and premature death. statistics show that one in three adults in the republic of croatia is a smoker, and the average croatian smoker smokes 20-30 cigarettes a day. it is estimated that in croatia, smoking kills about 14,000 people a year. in order to better protect human health, international cooperation, in particular the exchange of technology, knowledge and financial assistance and the provision of joint expertise, is necessary in order to establish effective tobacco control programmes, taking into account the culture of the community concerned, but also social, economic, political and legal factors. the protocol can contribute to public health and the international fight against illicit trade in tobacco products, as well as to tax avoidance and organised crime. for the above reasons, i have supported this recommendation.

‒ the who framework convention on tobacco control is the world's first health treaty. it was designed in response to the global epidemic of tobacco dependence to tackle some of its causes, including the illicit trade in tobacco products. it entered into force on 27 february 2005 and has so far been acceded to by 180 parties. the protocol to eliminate illicit trade in tobacco products adopted by the conference of the parties on 12 november 2012 in seoul is based on article 15 of the fctc. the protocol is currently the only multilateral regulatory initiative that exists in this area. the illicit trade in tobacco products, and in particular the smuggling of cigarettes, is a criminal activity that poses a serious threat to public health. it undermines tobacco control policies and increases the availability of often cheaper tobacco products. in addition, it causes huge revenue losses for the eu due to unpaid taxes and customs duties. the loss of revenue for the eu and its member states is estimated at more than eur 10 billion per year. that is why i welcome the decision of the european parliament to give its consent to the conclusion of the agreement.

written. ‒ the purpose of the protocol is to combat illicit trade in tobacco products. any practice or conduct associated with the production, receipt, distribution, possession, sale, purchase that is prohibited by law is considered to be illicit trade. the tobacco industry has a responsibility to effectively address the illicit trade in tobacco products and to mitigate the irreconcilable conflict between its interests and those of public health. the protocol provides for the supervision of the tobacco chain to be carried out by a series of measures. it also provides for a global monitoring regime to enable the exchange of information at the level of the world health organisation, leading to the establishment of a national and regional monitoring system. i support the adoption of this protocol because i consider that it encourages and strengthens international cooperation, encourages the exchange of information, technical and police cooperation and mutual legal and administrative assistance.
