mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european union must act against the epidemic of obesity and related diseases as it is probably the greatest long-term threat to public health. according to the world health organization, over 50% of europeans are overweight, and we have the worst death rate in the world from cardiovascular disease, diabetes and cancer. the main reason for this is the diet and the unhealthy composition of the food. it is estimated that cardiovascular diseases kill 660 000 people in the european union every year, and industrial trans fats have been identified as the single most harmful ingredient. their share in the food produced is legally limited by the commission because the common market makes national measures ineffective. even the big food companies have realized this and are reducing the amount of trans fats in their products. i supported this resolution and i hope that the commission will act as soon as possible because the price we pay in terms of the cost of treatment and illness and human lives is simply too high.
written. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament's resolution on trans-fatty acids primarily because of the negative health effects they have. this is a major problem among young people who frequently consume fast food and thus consume excessive amounts of these cheap but harmful acids. the second problem is that a large percentage of consumers are not aware of what trans-fatty acids are and what the negative consequences are. i therefore support the proposal to limit the amount of these in products and to launch information campaigns on the health effects of trans-fatty acids. i think olive oil, for example, could be a healthy and effective alternative to trans-fatty acids.
written. ‒ a high consumption of industrially produced partially hydrogenated vegetable oils is associated with increased risks of cardiovascular disease, infertility, endometriosis, gallstones, alzheimer's disease, diabetes, obesity and some cancers. the efsa recommendation is to reduce trans-fatty acid intake as much as possible within a diet that meets nutritional needs. international studies show that policies aimed at limiting the amount of trans fatty acids in food lead to a reduction in the level of trans fatty acids without increasing the total fat content, and eu legislation does not prescribe the amount of trans fatty acids in food products or require their labelling. the corresponding decisions to reduce the level of intake of industrial trans-fatty acids should be taken at eu level. since consumers are not aware of the negative health effects of trans fatty acids, mandatory labelling of trans fatty acids is an important step towards reducing the intake of trans fatty acids among european citizens, and i therefore supported this resolution.
written. ‒ i supported the resolution asking the european commission to propose within two years a legal limit on the level of industrial trans-fatty acids in food products. trans fat consumption has been linked to increased risks of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, infertility, gallstones, endometriosis, alzheimer's disease, and some forms of cancer. in addition, in view of the increasing prevalence and spread of obesity, including in children, i welcome the efforts of the european parliament to adopt, in cooperation with the commission, the necessary acts to reduce the level of dietary intake of trans-fatty acids. although croatia has regulations that limit the level of trans-fatty acids in food, the single market requires that this problem be regulated at european level. that is where i see the value of this initiative of the european parliament. trans-fatty acids are present in food of natural origin and their industrial production is exclusively linked to reducing food production costs. a balanced and natural diet of quality agricultural products is once again proving to be the right choice, while various forms of "artificial" and industrially produced food, often motivated solely by profit, are once again proving harmful to health.
written. ‒ this resolution only applies to industrially produced fatty acids, the consumption of which is associated with increased risks of cardiovascular disease, infertility, diabetes, obesity, some forms of cancer, etc. efsa, who and fda agree on the harmfulness of trans fatty acids to human health. the eu has so far not regulated the content of trans fatty acids in food products or required their labelling. however, in certain member states such as denmark, austria, latvia and hungary there is legislation limiting the proportion of trans-fatty acids in food products. the danish authorities have also provided evidence that the use of the new legislation is likely to lead to a reduction in the number of deaths from cardiovascular disease. it is necessary to introduce precisely such measures at union level. the introduction of mandatory labelling of trans-fatty acids on products is an insufficient mechanism compared to mandatory restrictions, as consumers are not aware of the negative impact of trans-fatty acids. s&d has warned of this problem before. parliament is now quite united in its message to the commission and i believe that the commission must as soon as possible set legal limits on the values of industrial trans-fatty acids, because only such a solution can save tens of thousands of lives a year.
written. ‒ trans-fatty acids are naturally found in food obtained from mammals, in some plants, and in human breast milk. however, most of the trans fatty acids consumed are industrially produced. there is evidence of health risks associated with the consumption of trans fatty acids and the cause of obesity in humans. i support the motion for a resolution on trans-fatty acids (2016/2637 ((rsp)) as informing about the harmful effects of industrial trans-fatty acids and limiting their use can prevent health risks for european citizens.
written. ‒ since we have been elected by our constituents to represent their interests at eu level, their well-being should be our primary objective in all respects, with particular attention to protecting their health. this resolution points to the harmfulness of trans-fatty acids used in food products in order to contribute to the desired coexistence of food products and ensure a long shelf life. high intakes of trans fatty acids are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, including coronary heart disease, which is responsible for around 14% of the overall mortality rate in the european union. it is clear from the above arguments that trans fatty acids are only a cheap ingredient in the production process and i believe that it is not enough to provide consumers with information on trans fatty acids and to promote healthier food choices, but we must also take concrete steps to protect our health. i therefore supported the call to the european commission to propose restrictions on the use of trans-fatty acids in food in order to protect public health.

written. ‒ during the first two and a half months of the state of emergency, the authorities closed down around 150 media outlets, leaving more than 2,300 journalists without jobs. furthermore, the police arrested at least 99 journalists and writers, most of whom have not been charged to date. the detained journalists have been denied their legal rights, while several journalists have reportedly been abused in prison. journalists are also targeted for administrative sanctions, which include the confiscation of passports. even family members of journalists, even if not themselves under investigation, are subject to threats and administrative sanctions. foreign journalists, on the other hand, have been deported from turkey. we therefore join the calls on the turkish authorities to immediately release all imprisoned journalists in the absence of credible evidence of criminal activity, to lift the administrative sanctions imposed on journalists and to refrain from threatening the family members of suspected journalists. we also call on the turkish authorities to prevent violence against suspects and to investigate allegations of torture of detained journalists. we also ask that the closed media be allowed to continue to operate and to be independent in their work.

mr. president, i want to be absolutely clear right from the start. after analyzing many arguments for and against, i will advocate for the abolition of the so-called summer time. the reasons for the recent introduction of daylight saving time are no longer the arguments they once were. a hundred years ago, when wartime time was first introduced, the main argument was to save the key energy source, coal. of course, the way of life was completely different from today. today, fortunately, we have more and more renewable energy sources, and of course our daily lives have completely changed. they may mention our heating and cooling habits or, even more drastically, our transportation habits. so it's clear that energy conservation is no longer a strong enough argument to change the clocks throughout the year. i think we need to start today with the indisputable fact, the proven harmful effects of the human biorhythm on changing weather. this is especially evident in the elderly. it has also been shown to affect animal welfare. in addition, changing the timing often creates additional communication chaos. human life, along with animal welfare, should be put before economic interests. if we never had knowledge of daylight saving time and its consequences, we now undoubtedly do. that should be the main argument in this debate and the main argument for abolishing time change. an online survey of 1,500 respondents conducted by our colleague, mr. škrlec, shows that as many as 85% of citizens in croatia are against changing the time. they claim there's virtually no energy savings. so i call on the commission and on you, commissioner, to simply take account of this virtually unanimous thinking in this parliament and to amend the directives and to stop double counting the time.

vice-president of the commission. – madam president, honourable members, i welcome the report on increasing the effectiveness of development cooperation. it provides an important input to the second high-level meeting of the global partnership for effective development cooperation (gpedc). the development effectiveness agenda and gpedc marked a shift from aid to development effectiveness, moving the focus from official development assistance flows to broader development partnerships and actors. five years after the forum held in busan, korea, it is a good moment to assess the implementation of commitments taken and to discuss how effective development cooperation can best contribute to implementing the 2030 agenda on sustainable development and the addis ababa action plan on financing for development. the eu should continue to lead and move these agendas forward. the new european consensus for development, which will guide the eu and member states’ development policy in the years ahead will help develop effectiveness at its heart. we need to consider not just what we do, but how we do it. important steps have been taken to advance a more strategic and coordinated eu approach, for example by advancing a joint programming of eu and member states development assistance; maximising our collective impact and minimising overlaps; increasing transparency of aid and mutual accountability; measuring results on the basis of our new results framework; promoting ownership of the development priorities by partner countries, and addressing conflict and fragility. nevertheless, in order to implement the 2030 agenda successfully, more needs to be done at both eu and global level. the commission believes that the global partnership should strengthen the political momentum behind effective development cooperation and support implementation of these principles and commitments at country level. it should promote multi-stakeholder platforms at country level and the use of available data to enhance dialogue. if strategically developed and used, the global partnership can indeed provide added value to other international fora in the implementation, thus contributing to the follow-up process of the 2030 agenda. the report rightly recognises that the specific value added of the global partnership is in its inclusive and multi-stakeholder character, and stresses the need for all actors to be involved in moving the effectiveness agenda forward. in order to become a true partnership of all relevant actors, the involvement of parliaments, civil society organisations, local authorities and private sector is essential. averting situations of fragility also entails closer cooperation, notably with humanitarian actors, to build the resilience of vulnerable populations. the private sector and providers of south-south cooperation can make a huge contribution to achieving the sustainable development goals. we need to improve our ways of working in partnership, such as through the recently proposed external investment plan and dialogues with southern providers. we also need to see action and commitments from these actors. we would like the outcome document of the nairobi high-level meeting to include their ideas on how they will implement the principles in practice. the global partnership brings a special perspective by focusing on relations between development actors, but also through monitoring the progress of the implementation of principles and commitments. the recently published 2016 progress report entitled ‘making development cooperation more effective’ is a valuable source of evidence-based information to stimulate policy dialogue at country, regional and international level. to conclude, i would like to stress the commission’s commitment to development policy principles – results, transparency, country ownership and inclusive partnerships. we call on all development partners to ensure that the nairobi high level meeting further enhances the contribution of the global partnership to the 2030 agenda. the commission is committed to keeping the european parliament and its relevant committees informed on the advancement of global partnership.

written. ‒ i voted in favour of the draft legislative resolution of the european parliament on the proposal for a council directive amending the directive on access to information by tax authorities for the prevention of money laundering, because i believe that there is a need to ensure more efficient, clearer and fairer taxation in the european union. i support measures that give tax authorities access to all the information they need to carry out their duties effectively. this shall provide access to the mechanisms, documents, procedures and information necessary to strengthen the european and international transparency framework and to prevent money laundering. in addition, it is necessary to exchange information automatically between tax authorities and to strengthen international cooperation in this area.
the commission shall adopt implementing acts laying down the conditions for the application of this regulation, including the conditions for the application of the provisions of this regulation. that directive introduces a global standard for the automatic exchange of information on financial accounts in tax matters within the union. the commission shall adopt implementing acts laying down the rules on the reporting of financial account holders to the member state in which the account holder is resident. cases such as swissleaks and the panama papers have once again confirmed the need for greater tax transparency and closer coordination between institutions, and given the global nature of anti-money laundering activities, international cooperation is key to effectively and efficiently combating such activities. the existence of an automatic, mandatory and permanent exchange of information in the field of taxation between the different competent authorities is essential to ensure maximum transparency and to obtain a basic instrument for preventing and combating fraud of all kinds. the mandatory automatic exchange of information on tax matters is internationally recognised as the most effective instrument in the service of international tax transparency at the level of the g20, the oecd and the european union. i consider that the fight against tax evasion and tax avoidance is an absolute priority for the union, and i have therefore supported this report.
written. ‒ i support this proposal to amend directive 2011/16/eu on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation by introducing measures to allow tax authorities to have consistent access to information on money laundering. the panama papers scandal, which exposed the massive concealment of money in so-called offshore accounts, has shown us that we need to insist on greater transparency and control. offshore companies operate in legal transactions without major assets, and for registration they only need personal data, an open giro account and a postal envelope. they are usually opened in countries with low tax rates. the way these companies operate in these countries allows their founders to move money abroad and thus avoid paying taxes. this in itself distorts the tax system of the country of residence of the recipient of those services and leads to large-scale tax fraud. the purpose of the report is to enable tax authorities to have constant access to anti-money laundering information to perform their duties in monitoring the proper application of directive 2011/16/eu, and the automatic exchange of documents and information is requested.

written. ‒ i voted for the green paper on retail financial services because i believe it is important that the new proposals benefit all eu consumers to ensure that the retail financial services market works for everyone. the market is still quite underdeveloped and highly fragmented in the eu, which requires effective measures to unlock its full potential as a single market and to facilitate innovation for the benefit of end-users. the green paper report, which i voted for, is about financial services offered to citizens seeking cross-border services, especially in relation to the rapid changes brought about by digitalisation and innovation in financial technologies. there is great potential to create new and better financial products, reduce transaction costs, facilitate access to finance, security and data protection.
written. ‒ retail finance provides a range of services that are important to citizens: current accounts, pensions and savings, mortgages and financing of other purchases, health or accident insurance and property insurance. the green paper explores the current state of the single market for retail financial services, as well as the recent trend towards digitalisation, and the need to act at eu or national level to overcome the barriers currently stopping consumers and businesses from moving across borders. the green paper is an opportunity to propose a european market for financial services such as insurance, credit, electricity and savings accounts and other retail investments and how to open up to these services, thereby creating better conditions for consumers and businesses, while maintaining a level of consumer and investor protection. it also examines the obstacles faced by consumers and businesses in using the single market. for all of the above, i supported the green paper on retail financial services.

development package. now you will ask me what for – exactly, because it is not only our work on security and defence that goes forward on the implementation of the global strategy, but it is all the development and also vice-versa. so i would like to underline the fact that the debate we are having on this particular issue does not happen in a vacuum but, on the contrary, in full conjunction and in full coherence with the work that we do on other strands of work. on defence in particular, there is today a momentum for deep and decisive changes. as i was preparing for this debate today i was remembering that, in my hearing in athens in october 2014, before taking office, we discussed this issue at length and, in particular, i asked my team to print out the minutes of that hearing and i remembered, in particular, a question that arnaud danjean asked me at that time and i replied: je vais jouer mon rôle de chef de l'agence européenne de défense, je vais visiter les missions, je vais beaucoup travailler avec les ministres de la défense, parce que dans ce cadre, il est important, bien entendu, de travailler avec nos autres partenaires, notamment l'otan mais pas seulement. cependant, il y a un potentiel dans le traité de lisbonne qui n'est pas forcément exploité, et je vais voir dans les cinq prochaines années si les conditions politiques pour l'utiliser enfin sont réunies. i think we are actually there. i think that, after two years of my term of office, not necessarily for personal reasons, or in relation to personal skills, but because of political conditions. first of all, because our citizens see security as a top priority, and also because member states see the need to work seriously on security and defence, i think we are there: at the political juncture where advancing on security and defence is finally possible. as we all know, defence falls primarily within member states’ competences, and that is why, for each step we take, we receive input from member states. all proposals are discussed extensively with all 28 member states. let me stress this: we are still 28 member states, and all decisions we take in this field are unanimous decisions, including the one we took last week, and this process led to the council conclusions adopted last monday, based on the implementation plan that i presented to ministers as a concrete follow-up to the eu global strategy. these conclusions formulate the consensus among, as i said, 28 member states about our joint level of ambition, and open a whole new chapter for our security and defence. i am glad to see, too, that our views are almost identical in all fields. your report addresses all the critical issues we have been working on and its overall approach matches perfectly with our broader package of proposals concerning european security and defence. the report focuses on a more robust csdp, on our integrated approach to crises, on our cooperation with nato and other partners, and on the european defence industry. if you look at the three proposals we are presenting, they are perfectly in line with your recommendations. it is a package, the one we are working on now on security and defence of the european union – a package including three different sets of proposals, three different pillars. those are the implementation plan on security and defence, which i presented and which was adopted last week, and also the implementation of the eu-nato joint declaration that we signed in warsaw, and the commission defence action plan on our defence industry. so, just to give you a sense of how fast and concretely things are moving: on monday last week the foreign affairs and defence ministers together adopted the implementation plan on security and defence. the day after that, on tuesday last week, we met again with nato secretary general jens stoltenberg to progress cooperation with nato. we presented a joint set of 40 proposals to turn into concrete actions – the principles of the warsaw declaration we signed jointly in july. these two processes are obviously autonomous and independent but running side by side, because we both share the assessment that a stronger europe makes nato stronger. it is clear that in practice there is no contradiction between europe’s strategic autonomy, which we assert, and our commitment to our long-term partners. for nato members, nato will remain the cornerstone of collective defence. strategic autonomy means, first and foremost, the ability to be a reliable partner, to care about our own security at home and in the neighbourhood, to take our fair share of responsibility and to be a genuine security provider. this will also require stronger european defence capabilities, as the report rightly points out, and this need is also addressed by the implementation plan. i will get to that in a minute, but let me first mention the european defence action plan, which will focus on overcoming the current fragmentation of the market and increasing the competitiveness of the european defence industry. linked to that is the preparatory action for defence research to be launched next year. this can be a real game changer for our industry. the starting point is one of our most successful experiences, the horizon 2020 research programme, which, to date, covers civilian and dual-use technologies. a continent-wide joint research programme on defence would be a natural extension of horizon 2020. we have immense potential in terms of joint research programmes on defence, economies of scale and more predictable timeframes for investments. to develop the technologies of the future, it is very clear to all of us, i believe, that we need to start investing now, but a big part of our work can also deliver concrete results in a shorter timeframe, and, with the implementation plan on security and defence, we are moving fast in this field too. so, with last week’s decision – and i am sorry you had to change the report – member states agreed to raise the level of ambition of our security and defence policies. we have agreed that we need to protect our citizens through our external action. and let me clarify here that this is not about having an article-5-style approach: as i said, collective defence is not for the european union, we are not a military alliance, but we need to use our external action and instruments to protect our citizens, including at home. we need to strengthen our neighbours and partners to prevent new conflicts, and we need to respond to crises in an effective manner. so the implementation plan includes 13 concrete proposals to match this new level of ambition that we determined together and agreed upon, as well as a clear timeframe for action. it will now be up to the european council in december – when i will present this new level of ambition and the various options for putting it concretely on the table – to discuss and agree on the proposals. but let me mention a few of these proposals, as, again, they are perfectly in line with your report. i will mention a few of them, not all of them, but enough to give you a flavour of what we are working on. firstly, more efficient defence spending. most of the narrative turns around the need to increase our spending. however, when you look at the numbers, you see that europeans spend 50% of the united states’ budget on defence, yet in terms of output we achieve 15% compared to what we spend. so we have a budget gap, but we also have an output gap that we have to look at, and here i have proposed a coordinated annual review of defence spending to promote joint programmes among member states and economies of scale. secondly, better rapid response. we know well that reacting fast is, at times, the only way to react effectively. time is not neutral when one is reacting to crises. we already have first-class civilian experts and we need to be able to deploy them quickly, but this is also about our battle groups, which next year will have been in existence for 10 years. the plan proposes the removal of the political, technical and – let me stress – financial obstacles that have so far prevented the battle groups’ deployment, including through modularity. thirdly, the joint planning and conduct of non-combat missions. let me delete the word ‘non-combat’, as we do not have combat missions, we have executive and non-executive missions. anyway, the joint planning and conduct of our missions and operations. the european union is currently deploying 17 military and civilian operations, but to make them more effective we need to improve the coordination among them. the plan seeks to fill the gaps and to ensure that missions are planned and carried out in a coherent way. this is not about creating big, new operational, shape-style headquarter. that is not what we need today: what we need today is to streamline our current structures and make them work better. we already have headquarters running our missions and operations, so this is not about creating something new: it is about using our resources better in a more effective and efficient manner and, as i said, streamlining and making more operational the coordination of our various missions and operations. the last, though certainly not the least, of these few examples is that of new permanent-structure cooperation. here again we come to the issue of making full use of the treaties, as i said two years ago. a single system of permanent-structure cooperation is an option that is there in the treaties. i suggest that we look into it for those member states that are willing to undertake higher commitments on security and defence. a single pesco would be one of the options on which i will work with a view to proposing this to member states. for all these proposals i am presenting concrete measures, and i would like to stress that this is very concrete and, at the same time, ambitious yet pragmatic work we are doing. it is not strategic thinking – we did that exercise last year. now it is about turning this vision into action. we are not getting into a revision of the treaties, which would take years and i am personally not sure it would lead us very far at this moment. we are not working on the creation of an eu army, only to get stuck in a never-ending ideological debate – and, by the way, not even nato has a nato army. as all those who deal with defence issues know very well, member states have one set of forces, which they can use either nationally, in nato, in the european union, in the united nations or in other formations. we have already set up our vision, as i said, with the global strategy: we are now turning the vision into concrete, effective and immediate action, and i would like to stress that this immediate action is being taken together in unity. i see the political will from member states to do this. i see the will finally to move towards a european union of security and defence. our fathers and mothers and grandfathers and grandmothers tried this in the 1950s, and we know how the story ended: the lisbon treaty gave us instruments we did not use. probably, the priority of managing the economic and financial crisis has since distracted us from security issues. i believe that now is the time for us to get serious and work effectively in this direction, and i expect the european parliament to keep supporting and contributing to this process, as it has been doing, in a very useful manner.

written. ‒ i voted in favour of the draft legislative resolution of the european parliament on the proposal for a directive of the parliament and of the council on the reduction of national emissions of certain atmospheric pollutants and amending directive 2003/35/ec, because the deterioration of human health and environmental pollution are problems that know no borders, directly affect all citizens of the union and require urgent action. air pollution has a direct and powerful impact on premature death, rising health costs, ground-level vegetation diversity, plant growth, and a host of other problems. the targets set for reducing air pollution are still not met and concrete measures are needed to achieve long-term and consistent union targets. i support new emission limits for 2020 and 2030, and the development of national air pollution control programmes. furthermore, i believe that smarter and more efficient legislation is needed to reduce the administrative burden on member states and businesses, and to improve the exchange of information at all levels. in this context, it is necessary that member states are clearly informed of the state of play of their action and that they initiate concrete corrective actions in the event of non-compliance with the commitments.
written. ‒ this proposal for a directive should contribute effectively to the achievement of air quality objectives set out in union legislation and to the mitigation of the effects of climate change by reducing emissions of short-lived climate pollutants, improving synergies with union climate and energy policies and ensuring that there is no overlap between existing legislation, while improving air quality worldwide. however, the eu is still far from achieving its long-term objective of adhering to the recommended pollution limits under the 2005 air quality guidelines. in 2013, the commission published the long-awaited clean air package, which sets out measures to ensure that existing targets are met in the short term and sets new air quality targets for the period up to 2030. this report emphasises the fact that better regulation and environmental protection are not mutually exclusive and that this directive should therefore be aligned with the other pillars of eu policy. the commission should be able to assess the impact of the proposed amendments on the environment and the environment protection of the union's forests, and to take into account the impact of the amendments proposed by the commission.
written. ‒ the programmes required by the directive must take into account the cost-effectiveness of emission reduction measures, the priorities of concrete policy measures aimed at reducing the health risks to vulnerable groups of people, quantify additional reductions in greenhouse gas emissions to meet the 2030 world health organisation targets, support the shift of investment towards clean and efficient technologies and sustainable production with the help of fiscal incentives. the commission shall assess progress in reducing air pollutants according to the world health organisation's clean air scale by 2025 at the latest. the directive contributes to the union's long-term objective of achieving a level of air quality that does not lead to significant adverse effects on human health and the environment, to the achievement of the union's biodiversity and ecosystem objectives by reducing the levels and deposition of certain atmospheric pollutants, to the achievement of the air quality objectives of union legislative acts, to the mitigation of the impacts of climate change by reducing emissions of short-lived climate pollutants and to improving synergies with the union's climate and energy policies. in the light of the above, i supported the amendments adopted by the european parliament on 28 october 2015 on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the reduction of national emissions of certain atmospheric pollutants and amending directive 2003/35/ec following reconsideration by the standing committee on the environment, public health and food safety.
written. ‒ the european union has made significant progress in the last 20 years in the area of anthropogenic emissions and air quality thanks to ambitious policies. however, environmental and human health risks remain. this directive is an important step in the fight against air pollution. the directive should contribute to the achievement of air quality objectives set out in union legislation and to the mitigation of the effects of climate change by reducing emissions of short-lived climate pollutants while improving air quality at global level and improving synergies with union climate and energy policies. poor air quality causes over 400,000 premature deaths a year and its economic costs are estimated at between 300 and 900 billion euros each year. this agreement aims to halve the number of premature deaths by 2030. 90% of europe's citizens live in cities and are exposed to air pollution levels that are harmful to human health. many vulnerable socioeconomic groups are particularly exposed. measures to tackle dangerous pollutants are urgently needed in all sectors. eu governments must take action to ensure that economic sectors, including agriculture, act responsibly on the substances they release into the atmosphere. i call on member states to act as soon as possible and to fully implement the directive and take further steps in our joint fight against air pollution.
written. ‒ air pollution is a local, pan-european and global problem because air pollutants emitted in one country can easily reach other countries, causing or contributing to poor air quality. therefore, stronger efforts to address this problem are urgently needed. the european union is working at many levels to reduce exposure to this problem: through legislation, cooperation with the sectors responsible for pollution, national and regional authorities, non-governmental organisations and research. the revised thematic strategy on air pollution sets new strategic targets for the period up to 2030 to achieve the union's objectives, including measures to reduce emissions of nitrogen dioxide, nitrous oxide, ammonia, fine particulate matter and the number of cases and premature deaths from air pollution-related diseases. however, aviation emissions from take-off and landing and marine emissions are still not taken into account. it is necessary to amend directive 2003/35/ec of the european parliament and of the council in order to ensure consistency with the 1998 aarhus convention on access to information, public participation in decision-making and access to justice in environmental matters. the enhanced efforts of all member states are a key enabler of this process in reducing emissions of climate pollutants and improving air quality globally.

written. ‒ i have expressed my support for the proposal for a european parliament resolution on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the reduction of national emissions of certain atmospheric pollutants and amending directive 2003/35/ec. the report offers a better solution using modern technologies that will increase the efficiency of the control of emissions of air pollutants. the report defined the shortcomings of the existing regulations in a substantive way, with an emphasis on the cost-effectiveness of measures to reduce pollutant emissions and on the establishment of adequate policy measures that will reduce health risks. taking into account that pollutants affect the entire ecosystem, additional financial resources from the budget of the european union should be mobilised to achieve adequate air quality. the report insists that the environmental policy of the european union be fully aligned with positive legislative solutions. the commission has also taken into account the fact that the commission has not yet adopted a legislative proposal on the subject.
written. ‒ while the eu's policies are largely focused on preserving and protecting the environment, it can be seen that much of the focus is on tackling climate change, while far less attention is paid to air quality. considering that poor air quality contributes to premature mortality, disease, loss of productivity, loss of crop yields, and damage to buildings, it is clear that emissions of air pollutants are a health and environmental problem. i support the recognition in the report of the need to reduce the negative impacts and risks of air pollution on the environment and human health, but i believe that the introduction of new, higher limits will not achieve much as individual member states cannot achieve the targets set. i believe that it is first and foremost necessary for each member state to set targets that it will be able to actually meet, and i have accordingly abstained.

written. ‒ a resilient pension system includes a diverse range of products and effective supervisory practices. in the light of demographic trends and the state of national budgets, occupational pension schemes are a valuable complement to social security pension schemes. they are under pressure and we are increasingly relying on occupational pensions to supplement other forms of pension insurance. the institutions for occupational retirement provision play an important role in the long-term financing of the economy. they manage assets worth eur 2,5 trillion on behalf of some 75 million members and beneficiaries. despite the entry into force of directive 2003/41/ec, cross-border activity is restricted by differences in national, social and labour law. the new directive aims at achieving minimum harmonisation and does not prevent member states from maintaining or introducing additional provisions to protect members and beneficiaries, provided that those provisions are compatible with the obligations of member states under union law. member states should retain full responsibility for the organisation of their pension systems in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity. this directive aims to encourage member states to build sustainable occupational pension systems and to facilitate cross-border activity. it is important to ensure that older persons and persons with disabilities are not exposed to the risk of poverty and can enjoy a decent standard of living.

member of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, i would like to thank the committee on development and its chair, mrs mcavan, for putting energy high on the development agenda. european union development cooperation in sustainable energy is supporting developing countries to advance towards economic growth powered by sustainable, affordable, reliable and modern energy for all. the three objectives of our energy and development engagements are to address the lack of energy access, to increase renewable energy generation and to contribute to the fight against climate change while ensuring sustainable use of resources. specific attention is given to sub-saharan africa. half of the global population without access to energy lives in this region and demographics aggravate the issue, with repercussions for political stability and migration to europe. in order to achieve our ambition, three factors are critical for success. first is policy ownership at the highest level. the promotion of energy, in particular renewable energy, must be owned by the partners. in the current financial framework, energy is a focal sector in about 30 national and regional indicative programmes. the commission has signed, on behalf of the european union and together with several member states, 21 joint declarations on enhanced energy cooperation with developing countries’ partners. second is the creation of an enabling environment. through our technical assistance facility, the commission provides support to partner countries on improving governance, legal and regulatory reforms and capacity building. third is sufficient capital. the commission has advanced considerably in generating more funding from banks and the private sector. it is estimated that, through blending, eur 3.7 billion allocated for energy cooperation in the current multiannual financing framework period will leverage investments of eur 15 to eur 20 billion, or even more. earlier this year, the electrification financing initiative, the so—called ‘electrify initiative’, which is an innovative mechanism to leverage investments, generated through its first invitation for applications 290 proposals requiring eur 800 million of financial support to leverage a potential total investment amount of eur 8.5 billion. this illustrates the significant contribution it can make to reaching universal access to energy. the proposed external investment plan would be one more important step in this direction. our vision cannot be implemented by governments and the private sector alone. there is also an important role for the participation of civil society, as organisations with a long presence and relationships of trust with local populations can be excellent partners in the energy sector. likewise, women need to play a major role in the integration of renewable energies in local economies and everyday life. a gender window has been created in ‘electrify’ to stimulate and exploit further this potential. there are still important risks impeding the investments which are necessary to meeting sustainable development goal no 7 – among others political instability, current fluctuations and insufficient market sizes. the commission is working together with all stakeholders to set up the right conditions in order to mitigate such risks. finally, let me address one specific issue. as regards the 11th edf national indicative programme for eritrea, the preparations for the implementation of a solar mini-grid programme with a pro-poor focus are underway. they are fully in line with the preconditions and principles defined by the member states at the edf committee meeting in november 2015. i am fully aware of the parliament’s concerns. let me reconfirm that no 11th edf projects in the energy sector will be presented as long as there is not a substantial project in support of the implementation of the un-led universal periodic review recommendations for eritrea under the governance sector. progress in the field of human rights will have to be seen for the european union to engage further in eritrea by committing funds under the 11th edf.

mr. president, i'm going to draw a parallel. you know very well where i come from - i come from croatia, from istria and you know that i have been involved in politics in croatia for a very long time, more than 20, about 25 years, that i have been active in istria and that i have done a lot for the rural development of istria. i can say that in the early 90s, when we started to build infrastructure in istria, electricity and water were the key things. people were leaving the countryside in istria, which is the most western and, by some measures, perhaps the richest region of croatia, for the cities by the sea. they simply did not want to live in a village without electricity or running water. that was only 25 years ago, which is not that long ago. i draw this parallel because we have the same situation a little bit more globally -- we have the fact that we have no energy and no water. if we don't have energy and water, we don't have development. so what do we have? migrants coming to europe. this symbolism, the parallel i want to draw is very simple, very mundane and we all understand it very well. what do you do in a situation like this? i am a strong advocate of synergy between all the key players on the world stage. and by that, i mean primarily us, the european union, which is the most generous of all partners on our planet anyway, but i also mean those who have interests in africa, like the united states, china, russia, and possibly someone else. i think that a sincere cooperation of all the key players should be the goal of everyone to save the situation in africa and to allow the people of africa to have access to energy, water and everything they need in key infrastructure projects. if we approach it in this way, we can solve a lot of the problems we face today. individual efforts will probably yield some results, but i'm sure not as a synergy, if it's politically possible, because europe is the only key political factor that can bring together perhaps some incompatible elements and make significant, rapid and powerful strides in africa. the other thing i would like to suggest is that maybe we shouldn't give too much money directly to african countries. maybe we should give more money, but indirectly. by investing in infrastructure where our european industry will ultimately have its goals and benefits, we can avoid something that is known to happen, which is the issue of corruption. in african countries, and unfortunately in european countries, it's all over the place, and we know it very well. i'm also inclined to talk about more resources to invest in energy in african countries, such as solar and wind energy, and not to do, as my last and third message, those mistakes that we made in developing energy in europe. so that the more we go to renewable energy sources and even those local sources that will not be networked. and that's a good way to develop rural areas in the african region. with these ideas, commissioner, i want to congratulate you on your efforts and work and i trust you will make sure that at least part of it is realized.

written. regulation (eu) no 1286/2014 of the european parliament and of the council introduced a series of measures to improve investor protection and restore consumer confidence in the financial services sector. it requires the issuer of packaged retail investment products and investment insurance products to produce a key information document. on 14 september 2016, the european parliament objected to the delegated regulation adopted by the commission on 30 june 2016 and, together with the large majority of member states, called for the postponement of the date of application of regulation (eu) no 1286/2014 to 1 january 2016. the 12-month delay will provide the parties involved with an additional period to comply with the new requirements, which is why i supported this report.
written. i support the postponement of the date of application of regulation (eu) no 1286/2014 of the european parliament and of the council on documents for packaged retail investment products and investment insurance products. the commission should be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 concerning the definition of the concept of 'investment products' and the definition of the concept of 'investment products'. the existing disclosures of information to retail investors on such priips are inconsistent and often do not help retail investors to compare different products or to understand their features. the commission also found that the chinese exporting producers had not provided sufficient evidence to support their claim that the measures were in line with the market economy investor principle. the commission should also be able to assess the impact of the measures on the investor protection measures in the member states. different approaches to disclosure of information related to priips prevent the creation of a level playing field for different priip issuers and those advising on or selling those products, thereby distorting competition and leading to unequal levels of investor protection in the union. such diversity constitutes an obstacle to the establishment and smooth functioning of the internal market. the improvement of the transparency of priips offered to retail investors is an important measure for their protection and a prerequisite for restoring retail investor confidence in the financial market, in particular in the aftermath of the financial crisis.
‒ regulation (eu) no 1286/2014 was adopted on 26 november 2014 to improve the protection of retail investors investing in packaged retail investment products and investment insurance products. the commission has also taken into account the fact that the financial services sector is facing a significant increase in the number of new entrants. the issuer of packaged retail investment products and investment insurance products shall be required to produce a key information document. the authority has also been given the power to adopt regulatory technical standards specifying the elements of the key information document. the commission delegated regulation of june 2016 was rejected by the european parliament and invited the commission to review the provisions on multiple-choice priips and the provisions on best-case scenarios and the understanding alert. together with the council, parliament also requested a delay in the date of application of the regulation as smooth application of the regulation is not possible as long as technical standards are not in place. the new date of application of the regulation is 1 january 2018 and this one-year delay will allow the parties involved an additional period to comply with the new requirements.

written. ‒ i voted in favour of the recommendation for a draft council decision on the conclusion, on behalf of the european union, of the agreement between the european union and the republic of kiribati on the short-stay visa waiver (12092/2015 c8-0253/2016 2015/0200(nle)), giving its consent to the conclusion of the agreement. relations between the european union and the republic of kiribati are governed by the partnership agreement between the members of the african, caribbean and pacific group of states of the one part, and the european union and its member states, of the other part, which provides for visa-free travel for citizens of the european union and the republic of kiribati to the territory of the other contracting party for a maximum period of 90 days in any 180-day period. it further strengthens economic and cultural relations and intensifies political dialogue on various issues, including human rights and fundamental freedoms. the republic of kiribati has made significant progress in respecting its international human rights obligations and in achieving internationally agreed goals, such as the millennium development goals.
written. ‒ relations between the european union and the republic of kiribati are governed by the cotonou partnership agreement. this agreement allows citizens of the european union and the republic of kiribati to stay without a visa in the territory of the other contracting party for a maximum of 90 days in any 180-day period. the agreement on the short-stay visa waiver is the result of efforts to deepen relations between the european union and the republic of kiribati and is of major political importance within the framework of the cotonou agreement. it also further strengthens economic and cultural relations and intensifies political dialogue on various issues, including human rights and fundamental freedoms. since i consider that the republic of kiribati does not pose any threat in terms of illegal migration or in terms of security, i have supported this recommendation.
written. i supported the draft decision on the conclusion of the eu-republic of kiribati agreement with a view to deepening the eu-republic of kiribati relations. it strengthens economic and cultural relations and intensifies political dialogue on a range of issues, such as human rights and fundamental freedoms. the agreement is expected to have a positive impact by facilitating travel for entrepreneurs, facilitating investment and stimulating the development of the tourism sector, which is very important as the economy of kiribati is primarily based on the services sector, which accounts for 66% of gdp, and the agriculture and fisheries sectors, which account for 25% of gdp. on the political level, the government of the republic of kiribati has made great progress in respecting its international human rights obligations and in achieving internationally agreed goals, such as the millennium development goals. in this regard, that agreement constitutes a positive sign of support for kiribati and allows for a balanced, regular and in-depth political dialogue on issues that remain a priority for the union. the visa waiver agreement not only enables citizens to derive full and tangible benefits from the kiribati-eu partnership, but also to actively participate in it and travel more easily at lower costs.

in writing. ‒ i support the motion for a resolution on the agreement between the european union and kiribati on the short-stay visa waiver. this agreement on the short-stay visa waiver is the result of efforts to deepen relations between the european union and the republic of kiribati and is of major political importance within the framework of the cotonou agreement. it also further strengthens economic and cultural relations and intensifies political dialogue on various issues, including human rights and fundamental freedoms. the agreement provides for the possibility for citizens of the european union and the republic of kiribati to stay without a visa in the territory of the other contracting party for a maximum period of 90 days in any 180-day period. the visa waiver applies to all categories of persons (holders of ordinary, diplomatic, official or special passports) whose purpose of travel does not involve the pursuit of a paid activity.

written. ‒ i voted for the report on the european union solidarity fund because it is one of the most concrete and tangible manifestations of the support that the european union can give to local communities. it is an important source of funding for local and regional governments to mitigate the effects of natural disasters. the unpredictability of disasters not only brings hardship to the affected population, but also raises the question of the speed of action of public authorities faced with unforeseen costs, therefore it is of the utmost importance to guarantee maximum transparency in the allocation, management and implementation of the european union solidarity fund.
written. ‒ following the tragic floods of 2002, the european union established the solidarity fund, which serves as a direct expression of the union's solidarity with countries affected by major natural disasters, and also applies to the acceding countries. the solidarity fund may assist member states where the total damage directly caused by elementary disasters exceeds eur 3 billion or 0,6% of the gross national income of the state, and there are also provisions for assistance in the event of minor regional disasters. the report aims to highlight the importance of the speed of the fund's intervention, the need for a policy of prevention and the need for complementarity between the fund and other european instruments, in particular cohesion policy. the rapporteur stresses that better cooperation between the different levels of decision-making can improve the transparency of the fund. i believe that the mechanisms for cooperation and complementarity in the work of the fund need to be improved, and i have therefore supported this report.
since its establishment in 2002, the european union solidarity fund (eusf) has proved to be a very useful and important instrument for mitigating the consequences of natural disasters by providing financial assistance to national governments and regional and local authorities in affected areas. in 14 years, member states have shown solidarity through this fund by assisting in 69 elementary disasters of different types and scales across europe, with 24 countries assisted by receiving assistance totalling eur 3,7 billion. over time, some adjustments and changes have been needed. the deadline for requesting aid has been extended to allow member states 18 months to use the funds from the date of payment, an advance of 10% has been introduced and some vague provisions have been made much clearer, all in line with numerous requests made over the years by the european parliament and local authorities. as this fund is the quickest way to help affected countries in the event of a disaster, i consider it important to consider, in the light of future reforms, the possibility of increasing the advance threshold from 10% to 15% and of reducing the deadlines for processing applications from six to four weeks - so that the necessary assistance can reach the affected areas as soon as possible.
written. ‒ the european union solidarity fund is an instrument to finance emergency operations following major natural disasters and regional emergencies in the eu, as well as in countries negotiating accession. it's used for a variety of natural disasters, such as earthquakes, floods, wildfires, storms, and the recent drought. the fund has so far mobilised a total of eur 3,8 billion for more than 70 disasters in 24 member states and accession countries. the number of disasters in the eu has increased significantly due to climate change and is becoming an increasingly serious problem, and therefore it is necessary to insist on a flexible instrument to provide adequate and rapid assistance to citizens affected by major disasters. in the light of future reforms, the commission is invited to consider the possibility of increasing the advance threshold from 10% to 15% and of reducing the deadlines for processing applications from six to four weeks. the possibility of setting an eligibility threshold for regional natural disasters of 1% of regional gdp should also be considered. we need to work on preventing potential disasters, creating opportunities for faster responses after disasters, and on greater transparency and better cooperation between different levels of decision-making. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council adopt a common position on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending regulation (ec) no 1260/1999 as regards the application of the principle of equal treatment for men and women as regards access to employment, vocational training and promotion, and working conditions.

written. the 2009 final report concluded that an international agreement binding the eu and the us to apply harmonised common data protection principles to transatlantic data transfers in the field of law enforcement would be the best solution. the purpose of the agreement is to ensure a high level of protection of personal information and to enhance cooperation between the united states and the european union in relation to the prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences, including terrorism. the working party on data protection, in its statement of 26 october 2016, pointed out that certain clarifications may be necessary to ensure that the level of protection of personal data provided by the framework agreement is fully in line with eu law. in order to ensure that the data subject is able to exercise his or her right of access to the data, the controller should be able to request the data subject to provide the data subject with a copy of the data subject's personal data. i supported the motion for a resolution because i consider that there is legal uncertainty as to the compatibility of the agreement with the provisions of the treaty and the charter of fundamental rights of the european union and that it is necessary to seek the opinion of the court of justice on the compatibility of the agreement with the treaties.
written. i consider it important to point out that the umbrella agreement does not provide a legal basis for transfers of personal data. the legal basis for data transfers is found in existing eu-us agreements, bilateral agreements between member states and the us, or in national laws regulating the exchange of personal data (e.g. international agreements on passenger name record, on the terrorist finance tracking program, or on mutual legal assistance). the data protection board shall be composed of representatives of the member states and of the commission. the agreement does not cover exchanges of data between national safety authorities, as they are not within the competence of the union. the privacy shield is a global agreement between the united states and the european union that protects the privacy of individuals and businesses, including by ensuring that they are protected from unauthorized access to their personal information. in the light of the foregoing, i do not consider it necessary to request the court of justice to give an opinion on the compatibility of the envisaged agreement with the treaties and have therefore not supported this motion for a resolution.

written. ‒ in 2011, the commission opened negotiations with the us on the protection of personal information in relation to criminal offences as part of the umbrella agreement. the purpose of this agreement is to ensure a high level of protection of the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals, in particular the right to privacy in the processing of personal data. the agreement does not provide a legal basis for the transfer of personal data, which is found in existing bilateral agreements between member states and the united states, but it complements the protection of those agreements and harmonises the rights of the data subject to the exchange. it also represents a major advance in the protection of personal data transferred between the eu and the us in the context of law enforcement activities. in addition, it does not restrict or infringe any rights of the data subject, as it does not constitute a legal basis for data transfers. this agreement shall apply to transfers of personal data between police authorities for the purposes of the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of criminal offences, including terrorism. it covers all transfers of data between those bodies, irrespective of the nationality or place of residence of the data subject. the agreement does not restrict rights but adds new legal protection to the existing data transfer frameworks in the context of eu-us police cooperation, which is why i supported this report.

written. the union's own resources system must ensure adequate resources for the orderly development of the union's policies, subject to strict budgetary discipline. the development of the own resources system can and should also contribute to the wider budget consolidation efforts undertaken in the member states and participate, to the greatest extent possible, in the development of union policies. the own resources ceiling should be equal to 1,23% of the total gni of the member state at market price for the appropriations for payments and a ceiling of 1,29% of the total gni of the member state should be set for the appropriations for commitments. in order to maintain the amount of financial resources made available to the union unchanged, it is appropriate to adjust those ceilings expressed as a percentage of gni. those ceilings should be adjusted as soon as all member states submit their data based on the european system of national and regional accounts (esa 2010). in the event of any amendments to the esa 2010 involving a significant change in the level of gni, the ceilings for own resources and committed appropriations should be readjusted. this decision should enter into force only after it has been approved by all member states in accordance with their respective constitutional provisions, thus fully respecting national sovereignty.

‒ italy, one of the most seismically active countries in the world, was struck by several devastating earthquakes between august 24 and october 20, 2016. the quakes killed 290 people, injured more than 400, and forced 100,000 citizens from their homes. in addition, the earthquakes have destroyed cities, damaged local and regional infrastructure, historical and cultural heritage and have a negative impact on agriculture, economy and tourism in the area. by this resolution, together with the other signatories, i called on the commission to take the necessary measures to provide effective and rapid support through the european union solidarity fund and to consider the possibility of activating the european fund for rural development and to use the funds received for the purpose for which they were intended by the italian government. i believe that this can greatly help the people affected by the earthquakes and help to bring about the much-needed recovery of economic and agricultural activities.
written. ‒ i support the motion for a resolution on the situation in italy after the earthquake. it is very important to show solidarity with the people of italy who have suffered enormous losses, both human and material. at this time, it is urgent to express concern about the large number of people who have lost their homes as a result of the devastating earthquakes. with the cold winter ahead, it is urgent to provide shelter for people whose homes have been destroyed by earthquakes. the solidarity fund must be used as soon as possible to provide financial assistance to the victims so that we do not have more victims of this natural disaster as a result of the slow response. in addition to taking clear action and reacting to the current situation in italy, it is important to plan preventive actions that would minimise or at least mitigate such disasters in the future. the importance and urgency of this situation was also demonstrated by the great courage of the rescue teams, volunteers and authorities at all levels in italy.

written. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the commissioner's declarations of financial interests guideline (2016/2080 ((ini))), as practice has shown that this issue needs to be regulated better. the commission notes that the commission has not provided any evidence that the financial situation of the beneficiary of the aid is such that it would be possible to assess the compatibility of the aid with the internal market. the commission has not received any comments from interested parties. it proposes a procedure for reviewing declarations of financial interests prior to the hearing of candidate commissioners, then a procedure for reviewing declarations of financial interests during the commissioners' mandate, and proposes to the commission the revision and the way of revising the 2011 code of conduct for commissioners. furthermore, the responsibilities, working methods, necessary documentation and the method of collection of the competent committee on legal affairs should be clearly and unambiguously defined in order to achieve the necessary transparency and efficiency in this regard.
written. ‒ the purpose of the review of the commissioners' declaration of financial interests is to examine whether the commissioners-designate are capable of exercising their duties with complete independence and to ensure the utmost transparency and accountability of the commission, in accordance with article 17 (3) of the treaty on european union, article 245 tfeu and the code of conduct for commissioners. the legal affairs committee shall be responsible for carrying out a comprehensive analysis of the declarations of financial interests, by means of a thorough examination aimed at establishing the credibility and accuracy of the content of the declarations of financial interests of the commissioner-designate. the problem is a poorly defined provision that does not cover the exact scope of the review carried out by this committee. parliament insisted that the committee issue guidelines in the form of recommendations or own-initiative reports to help reform the procedures for commissioner statements. the rapporteur proposes that the committee define a framework for the examination of declarations of financial interests, which would include the appointment of the new commission and the course of its mandate, and the transparency obligations to which its members are subject. any major change in the financial interests of a commissioner during his or her term of office and any reallocation of responsibilities between the members of the commission represents a new situation with regard to the possible existence of a conflict of interest and should be considered by parliament in the context of the examination procedure. i supported this report.
written. i support the motion for a resolution of the european parliament on the declarations of the commissioner's financial interests. i would remind you that the purpose of the examination of the declaration of financial interests of commissioners is to examine the ability of the commissioner-designate to act with complete independence and to ensure the utmost transparency and accountability of the commission, in accordance with article 17 (3) of the treaty on european union, article 245 tfeu and the code of conduct for commissioners. in this regard, i note that this should not be limited to the appointment of a new commission but should also apply to filling a vacancy due to the resignation of a commissioner, compulsory retirement or death of a commissioner, accession of a new member state or a substantial change in the portfolio of commissioners or their financial interests. i believe that this would give a more complete picture of the financial situation of the commissioner and give sufficient assurance that the person in question will carry out this responsible task with the utmost integrity. the code of conduct for commissioners should cover all financial interests and activities of the commissioner-designate and his/her spouse and should in no way be limited to those which could give rise to a conflict of interest.
written. ‒ strengthening ethics in the eu institutions is one of the pillars of european governance that must be trusted by our citizens. with the extension of the commission's political mandate by the treaty of lisbon, it has become even more important to have clear criteria and to respect the principle of transparency in the selection of commissioners. the confirmation by the legal affairs committee of the absence of a conflict of interest became an unavoidable prerequisite for the hearing of candidates. the commission shall inform the european parliament and the council of the outcome of the consultations. it is necessary to provide parliament with all the information requested when taking a decision on the suitability of a candidate, thereby ensuring an open and consistent assessment by the whole commission when appointed. i regret that the information in the current forms is limited and inadequate, without a detailed definition of conflict of interest and does not allow parliament to assess fairly and consistently the ability of candidates to perform their duties with complete independence and to ensure the commission's accountability. the commission should therefore be given sufficient time to carry out a thorough and thus effective analysis, with the right to additional hearings and to make the necessary clarifications where necessary. in this context, the concept of 'conflict of interest' must refer to objective and verifiable factors. i call for checks to be carried out in other procedures, not just the commission's appointment procedure.

‒ the legal affairs committee has produced a report which provides guidance on establishing clear rules for determining possible conflicts of interest of commissioners and clarifies the committee's remit. the report defines the meaning of 'conflict of interest' as any situation where private interests are opposed to the public interest and public interests affect or could affect the independence, impartiality and objectivity of the performance of the duties, and explains the procedure for reviewing declarations of financial interests before the hearings of candidate commissioners and during the commissioners' term of office. since i believe that the proposed procedures increase transparency and clarity of procedures, thus reducing ambiguity and facilitating the task of the members of the committee on legal affairs, i voted in favour of the adoption of this report.

written. ‒ offshore oil and gas activities are increasingly being carried out further offshore and in deeper waters. some of these are also in locations that are heavily dependent on tourism, such as the mediterranean. more than 90% of the oil and 60% of the gas produced in europe comes from offshore installations, and offshore exploration and exploitation activities are currently taking place or are planned in the territorial waters of 18 member states. the commission considers that the measures provided for in this decision are in accordance with the opinion of the committee established by article 15 (1) of regulation (eu) no 1380/2013, although breaches of coastal security are covered by criminal law in many countries, neither the definition of the offence nor the type and level of minimum sanctions are harmonised at eu level. the report stresses the importance of updating existing liability systems in member states to ensure that a potential accident in their territorial waters does not negatively affect the future of offshore oil and gas activities or the eu as a whole. it is necessary to promote a harmonised solution as regards the conditions for a mandatory financial guarantee. this should be done in such a way that the effectiveness of the 'cleaner pays' principle is not compromised by setting too low a minimum amount of guarantee or by limiting compulsory insurance to insurance products only, which is why i supported this report.
written. today, offshore activities are taking place or planned in the territorial waters of 18 member states, and more than 90% of the oil and 60% of the gas produced in the eu comes from offshore installations. i believe that the commission should work closely with the member states to ensure that the systems of compensation and financial guarantee for oil and gas exploration and exploitation in the eu are brought to a satisfactory level. i stress the importance of updating the existing liability systems in the member states to ensure that a possible accident in their territorial waters does not have a negative impact on the future of the coastal activities of those countries or on the future of the eu as a whole if the accident occurs in an area whose income is highly dependent on tourism. i therefore invite the commission to reconsider the need to introduce common eu standards for the system of claiming compensation and redress. the number of coastal installations is likely to increase in the future, in particular in the mediterranean and the black sea, which makes it urgent to fully implement directive 2013/30/eu and to ensure an appropriate legal framework for the management of all coastal activities. i would point out that, in accordance with article 191 tfeu, union policy on the environment must be based on the principles of precaution and prevention.
